Great to see you again! Today, I'd like to delve into your major legislative achievements and the challenges you faced along the way. Let's start with one of your most significant legislative accomplishments. Can you tell me about a particular piece of legislation that you are most proud of and why?

======= Document Begin =========
I had another source of worry, one I hadn’t allowed myself to dwell on but that had been in the back of my mind from the start. We’d now marshaled, defended, fretted over, and compromised on a 906-page piece of legislation that would affect the lives of tens of millions of Americans. The Affordable Care Act was dense, thorough, popular with only one side politically, impactful, and surely imperfect. And now it would need to be implemented. Late in the afternoon, after Nancy-Ann and I had worked through a round of last-minute calls to members heading off to vote, I stood up and looked out the window, across the South Lawn. “This law better work,” I told her. “Because starting tomorrow, we own the American healthcare system.” I decided not to watch the preliminary hours of speechmaking that went on in the House chamber, instead waiting to join the vice president and the rest of  the team in the Roosevelt Room once the actual voting began, around seventhirty p.m. One by one, the votes accumulated as House members pressed either “yea” or “nay” buttons on electronic voting panels, the running tally projected on the TV screen. As the “yeas” slowly ticked up, I could hear Messina and a few others muttering under their breath, “Come on…come on.” Finally the vote hit 216, one more than we needed. Our bill would go on to pass by a margin of seven votes. The room erupted in cheers, with people hugging and high-fiving as if they’d just witnessed their ball club winning with a walk-off home run. Joe grabbed me by the shoulders, his famous grin even wider than usual. “You did it, man!” he said. Rahm and I embraced. He’d brought his thirteen-year-old son, Zach, to the White House that evening to watch the vote. I leaned down and told Zach that because of his dad, millions of people would finally have healthcare if they got sick. The kid beamed. Back in the Oval, I made congratulatory calls to Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid, and when I was done, I found Axelrod standing by the door. His eyes were a little red. He told me he’d needed some time alone in his office following the vote, as it had brought back a flood of memories of what he and his wife, Susan, had gone through when their daughter Lauren had been first stricken with epileptic seizures. “Thanks for sticking with this,” Axe said, his voice choked up. I put my arm around him, feeling my own emotions swell. “This is why we do the work,” I said. “This. Right here.” I had invited everyone who worked on the bill up to the residence for a private celebration, about a hundred people in all. It was Sasha and Malia’s spring break, and Michelle had taken them to New York for a few days, so I was on my own. The evening was warm enough that we could mingle outside on the Truman Balcony, with the Washington Monument and Jefferson Memorial lit up in the distance, and I made an exception to my rule of weekday sobriety. Martini in hand, I made the rounds, hugging and thanking Phil, Nancy-Ann, Jeanne, and Kathleen for all the work they’d done. I shook hands with scores of junior staffers, many of whom I’d never met and who no doubt felt a little overwhelmed to be standing where they were. I knew they had toiled in the background, crunching numbers, preparing drafts, sending out press releases, and answering congressional inquiries, and I wanted them to know how critical their work had been. For me, this was a celebration that mattered. The night we’d had in Grant  Park after winning the election had been extraordinary, but it had been just a promise, not yet realized. This night meant more to me, a promise fulfilled
======= Document End =========

One of the legislative accomplishments I'm most proud of is the Affordable Care Act. It was a massive, 906-page piece of legislation that was set to impact tens of millions of Americans. The process was incredibly challenging, filled with compromises and intense political debates. I remember the tension on the day of the vote, watching the tally slowly climb in our favor, and the relief and celebration that followed when we secured enough votes. It was a moment of fulfillment, realizing that because of our efforts, millions would have healthcare coverage. This was why we did the work, to make such significant changes that directly improved lives.

The Affordable Care Act (ACA) is indeed a monumental achievement. Can you walk me through some of the key challenges you faced during the process of getting the ACA passed? What were some of the major obstacles, both politically and logistically, and how did you and your team overcome them?

Passing the Affordable Care Act was fraught with numerous challenges. Politically, it was a divisive issue, supported primarily by one side, which made it difficult to garner the necessary bipartisan support. We had to engage in extensive negotiations and compromises, constantly defending the bill's provisions to skeptics and critics. Logistically, the sheer volume and complexity of the legislation added to the challenge, as it was a 906-page document that required meticulous planning and understanding to ensure proper implementation.

The tension was palpable on the day of the vote. We made numerous last-minute calls to sway undecided members, and the anxiety of watching the vote tally slowly reach the needed majority was intense. Ultimately, the collective effort, dedication, and emotional investment of the team paid off, and the moment we secured the votes needed was one of profound relief and celebration. It was a testament to the hard work and commitment of everyone involved.

It sounds like an incredibly intense and rewarding experience. Can you share a specific moment or interaction during the ACA's journey that stands out to you? Perhaps a conversation with a colleague, a constituent, or an event that particularly highlighted the stakes or the impact of the legislation?

That's a touching and powerful story. It really brings home the personal and human aspect of legislative work. Shifting gears a bit, what were some of the key strategies you and your team employed to navigate the intense political opposition and ensure the ACA's passage? Were there any particular tactics or approaches that proved especially effective?

Returning to the White House, I suggested that we press our advantage by inviting the Four Tops and a bipartisan group of key congressional leaders to come to Blair House for an all-day meeting on healthcare. Once again, we arranged to have the proceedings broadcast live, this time through C-SPAN, and again the format allowed Republicans to make whatever points or ask whatever questions they wanted. Having been caught off guard once, they came prepared with a script this time. House GOP whip Eric Cantor brought a copy of the House bill, all 2,700 pages of it, and plopped it on the table in front of him as a symbol of an out-of-control government takeover of healthcare. Boehner insisted that our proposal was “a dangerous experiment” and that we should start over. John McCain launched into a lengthy harangue about backroom deals, prompting me at one point to remind him that the campaign was over. But when it came to actual policy—when I asked GOP leaders what exactly they proposed to help drive down medical costs, protect people with preexisting conditions, and cover thirty million Americans who couldn’t otherwise get insurance—their answers were as threadbare as Chuck Grassley’s had been during his visit to the Oval  months before. I’m sure that more people watched bowling that week than caught even five minutes of these conversations on TV, and it was clear throughout both sessions that nothing I said was going to have the slightest impact on Republican behavior (other than motivating them to bar TV cameras from my future appearances before their caucuses). What mattered was how the two events served to reinvigorate House Democrats, reminding them that we were on the right side of the healthcare issue, and that rather than focusing on the Senate bill’s shortcomings, they could take heart in how the bill promised to help millions of people. — BY THE BEGINNING of March, we had confirmed that Senate rules would allow us  to clean up parts of the Senate bill through reconciliation. We enhanced the subsidies to help more people. We trimmed the Cadillac tax to placate the unions and got rid of the twin embarrassments of the “Cornhusker Kickback” and “Louisiana Purchase.” Valerie’s public engagement team did great work lining up endorsements from groups like the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Medical Association, the American Nurses Association, and the American Heart Association, while a grassroots network of advocacy groups and volunteers worked overtime to educate the public and keep the pressure on Congress. Anthem, one of America’s largest insurers, announced a 39 percent rate hike, conveniently reminding people of what they didn’t like about the current system. And when the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops announced that it couldn’t support the bill (convinced that the bill’s language prohibiting the use of federal subsidies for abortion services wasn’t explicit enough), an unlikely ally arrived in the form of Sister Carol Keehan, a soft-spoken, perpetually cheerful nun who headed up the nation’s Catholic hospitals. Not only did the sixty-sixyear-old Daughter of Charity break with the bishops by insisting that passage of the bill was vital to fulfilling her organization’s mission of caring for the sick; she inspired the leaders of Catholic women’s orders and organizations representing more than fifty thousand American nuns to sign a public letter endorsing the bill. “I love nuns,” I told Phil and Nancy-Ann. Despite all this work, our tally still showed us at least ten votes shy of what we needed for passage. Public opinion remained sharply divided. The press had run out of fresh stories to write. There were no more dramatic gestures or policy  tweaks that might make the politics easier. Success or failure now depended entirely on the choices of the thirty or so House Democrats who represented swing districts, all of whom were being told that a vote in favor of the ACA could cost them their seat
======= Document End =========

================ Instruction End ================

To navigate the intense political opposition and ensure the ACA's passage, we employed several key strategies. One effective approach was hosting televised, bipartisan meetings at Blair House, which allowed both sides to discuss their views openly. This not only showcased the opposition's lack of solid alternatives but also reinvigorated our side by reminding us of the moral and practical merits of the ACA.

We also utilized the reconciliation process to make necessary adjustments to the bill, enhancing subsidies and removing unpopular provisions like the "Cornhusker Kickback." Additionally, we garnered endorsements from major medical associations and leveraged public discontent with the current system, highlighted by a significant rate hike announcement from a major insurer.

A crucial moment came when Sister Carol Keehan and other influential nuns supported the bill, countering opposition from the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops. This broad coalition of support, combined with relentless public and legislative engagement, helped us overcome the challenges and secure the necessary votes for passage.

It's clear that a multifaceted approach was essential in navigating the complexities of passing the ACA. The televised meetings, strategic use of the reconciliation process, and securing endorsements from influential groups all played pivotal roles. 

Can you elaborate on the impact of the public endorsements, particularly from Sister Carol Keehan and the nuns? How did their support influence the legislative process and public perception of the ACA?

The vast majority of your senior appointees, including cabinet secretaries, are weeks or sometimes months away from being confirmed. Across the White House complex, staffers can be seen securing the requisite IDs, asking where to park, learning how to operate the phones, figuring out where the bathrooms are, and schlepping boxes into the cramped warren of offices in the West Wing or the more capacious rooms in the nearby Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB), all while trying not to look completely overwhelmed. Great to see you again! Today, I'd like to delve into your major legislative achievements and the challenges you faced along the way. Let's start with one of your most significant legislative accomplishments. Can you tell me about a particular piece of legislation that you are most proud of and why?

One of the legislative accomplishments I'm most proud of is the Affordable Care Act. It was a massive, 906-page piece of legislation that was set to impact tens of millions of Americans. The process was incredibly challenging, filled with compromises and intense political debates. I remember the tension on the day of the vote, watching the tally slowly climb in our favor, and the relief and celebration that followed when we secured enough votes. It was a moment of fulfillment, realizing that because of our efforts, millions would have healthcare coverage. This was why we did the work, to make such significant changes that directly improved lives.

The Affordable Care Act (ACA) is indeed a monumental achievement. Can you walk me through some of the key challenges you faced during the process of getting the ACA passed? What were some of the major obstacles, both politically and logistically, and how did you and your team overcome them?

Passing the Affordable Care Act was fraught with numerous challenges. Politically, it was a divisive issue, supported primarily by one side, which made it difficult to garner the necessary bipartisan support. We had to engage in extensive negotiations and compromises, constantly defending the bill's provisions to skeptics and critics. Logistically, the sheer volume and complexity of the legislation added to the challenge, as it was a 906-page document that required meticulous planning and understanding to ensure proper implementation.

The tension was palpable on the day of the vote. We made numerous last-minute calls to sway undecided members, and the anxiety of watching the vote tally slowly reach the needed majority was intense. Ultimately, the collective effort, dedication, and emotional investment of the team paid off, and the moment we secured the votes needed was one of profound relief and celebration. It was a testament to the hard work and commitment of everyone involved.

It sounds like an incredibly intense and rewarding experience. Can you share a specific moment or interaction during the ACA's journey that stands out to you? Perhaps a conversation with a colleague, a constituent, or an event that particularly highlighted the stakes or the impact of the legislation?

A particularly memorable moment during the ACA's journey was right after the bill passed. I remember Rahm Emanuel brought his thirteen-year-old son, Zach, to the White House to watch the vote. After we secured the necessary votes, I leaned down to Zach and told him that because of his dad's efforts, millions of people would finally have healthcare if they got sick. Seeing his face light up with pride and understanding really underscored the personal impact of our work. It was a powerful reminder of why we push through such challenges—to make a real difference in people's lives.

That's a touching and powerful story. It really brings home the personal and human aspect of legislative work. Were there any particular tactics or approaches that proved especially effective?

To navigate the intense political opposition and ensure the ACA's passage, we employed several key strategies. One effective approach was hosting televised, bipartisan meetings at Blair House, which allowed both sides to discuss their views openly. This not only showcased the opposition's lack of solid alternatives but also reinvigorated our side by reminding us of the moral and practical merits of the ACA.

We also utilized the reconciliation process to make necessary adjustments to the bill, enhancing subsidies and removing unpopular provisions like the "Cornhusker Kickback." Additionally, we garnered endorsements from major medical associations and leveraged public discontent with the current system, highlighted by a significant rate hike announcement from a major insurer.

A crucial moment came when Sister Carol Keehan and other influential nuns supported the bill, countering opposition from the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops. This broad coalition of support, combined with relentless public and legislative engagement, helped us overcome the challenges and secure the necessary votes for passage.

Their support came at a crucial time when the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops had expressed opposition due to concerns about abortion services funding. Sister Carol's endorsement, representing a major healthcare organization and a large group of religious leaders, provided a moral and ethical validation of the ACA. It helped counteract some of the negative narratives and demonstrated broad and diverse support for the bill, reinforcing its importance for public health and moral responsibility. This endorsement not only helped sway public opinion but also reassured legislators, especially those in swing districts, about the bill's positive impact and moral grounding, aiding in securing the necessary votes for its passage.

Their endorsement underscored the ethical imperative of providing healthcare to millions of Americans, which was a powerful counterbalance to the opposition's arguments.
